children: Crude oil futures gave up early gains and settled lower Wednesday after the International Energy Agency agreed to speed up ​a planned release of oil stocks and prioritize diesel "given the current tightness" in markets.

The IEA's announcement follows Friday's hastily arranged meeting where an agreement was reached to release 100M barrels of oil to the market over the next four months, but the agency said Wednesday the release would come from the 400M-barrel stock release agreed in March and would not include additional barrels.
The IEA said 325M barrels of oil have been released to the market under the collective mechanism reached in March, with some countries having released greater volumes than initially pledged.

"Europe is ground zero for this whole supply crunch... and the releases address that and [take] some ⁠of the heat off the need for WTI to a degree. This should reduce some of the pressure on U.S. supplies," Again Capital's John ​Kilduff said in a note.

Crude futures fell Wednesday even as oil producers in the U.S. Gulf have shut in more than 510K bbl/day of crude production in response to Tropical Storm Isaias, the equivalent of ~25% of output in the region, according to the Marine Minerals Administration.

Traders also looked past fresh Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia, which damaged the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and an airport in the southern city of Abha, killing a total of three people and wounding 36 others.
Attacks in the Middle East have curbed ‌losses for Brent crude ⁠compared to US. crude futures, Kilduff said.
Ukraine hit two Russian oil facilities while Russia pounded Ukraine with waves of missiles and drones, killing at least 15 people, Ukrainian officials said.
Meanwhile, U.S. crude fell despite an unexpected weekly inventory draw

Commercial crude oil stocks excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell by 3.2M barrels to 424.1M barrels in the week ended October 2 and were 1% above the five-year average for the time of year, the EIA said.

Gasoline inventories posted a surprise 382K-barrel build to 204.7M barrels and were 6% below the five-year average, while distillate fuel stocks fell by 42K barrels to 105.1M barrels and were 12% below the five-year average for the time of year.

"Oil stockpiles remain tight but the crunch isn't clearly getting worse," David Russell of TradeStation said in a note, adding the inventory drop was the result of an adjustment, "so it may overstate the magnitude of the draw."
